english.heading: Seeds and Seed Sovereignty
body: Seed is where the next season begins.
When your household can save, store and share good seed, it carries more than a crop forward. It also carries the freedom to choose.
In this lesson, you will follow seed from the parent plant to the packet, the germination test and a neighbour’s hand.
Think about the crops in your area. Which ones do you already save seed from? Which seed do you buy? Which seed do you exchange?
Try to name at least one crop whose seed is already being saved in your area.

heading.text: Dipeo le Boikemelo ba Peo (seed sovereignty)

body.text: Peo ke moo sehla se tlang se qalang.
body.backTranslation: Seed is where the coming season begins.

body.text: Ha lelapa la hao le kgona ho boloka, ho baballa le ho arolelana peo e ntle, le fetisetsa ho feta sejalo feela. Hape le fetisetsa tokoloho ya ho ikgethela.
body.backTranslation: When your household can save, keep and share good seed, it passes on more than just a crop. It also passes on the freedom to choose for itself.

body.text: Thutong ena, o tla latela peo ho tloha semeleng sa motswadi ho ya paketeng, tekong ya hore na e a mela (germination test), le letsohong la moahisani.
body.backTranslation: In this lesson, you will follow a seed from the parent plant to the packet, to the test of whether it germinates (germination test), and to a neighbour's hand.

body.text: Nahana ka dijalo tsa sebaka sa heno. Ke dife tseo o seng o di bolokela peo? Ke peo efe eo o e rekang? Ke peo efe eo o e fapanyetsanang?
body.backTranslation: Think about the crops of your area. Which ones do you already save seed for? Which seed do you buy? Which seed do you swap?

body.text: Leka ho bolela bonyane sejalo se le seng seo peo ya sona e seng e bolokwa sebakeng sa heno.
body.backTranslation: Try to name at least one crop whose seed is already being saved in your area.

english.heading: Why Saving Seed Matters
body: Saving seed does not mean rejecting all bought seed. It means building practical choices.
Each crop you learn to save well removes one repeated purchase. It also begins a local record of what performs well in your soil and your season.
Think about the seed you buy again and again. Which repeated seed purchase costs your household the most each year?
Choose one crop from your planting list. Make it your practical starting point for seed saving. Do not try to save everything at once.

heading.text: Hobaneng ho Boloka Peo ho le Bohlokwa

body.text: Ho boloka peo ha ho bolele ho hana peo yohle e rekilweng. Ho bolela ho aha dikgetho tse sebetsang.
body.backTranslation: Saving seed does not mean refusing all bought seed. It means building choices that work.

body.text: Sejalo se seng le se seng seo o ithutang ho se bolokela peo hantle se tlosa theko e le nngwe e phetwang. Hape se qala tlaleho ya sebakeng sa heno ya se sebetsang hantle mobung wa hao le sehleng sa hao.
body.backTranslation: Every crop whose seed you learn to save well removes one repeated purchase. It also starts a local record of what does well in your soil and in your season.

body.text: Nahana ka peo eo o e rekang kgafetsa. Ke theko efe ya peo e phetwang e jang tjhelete e ngata ka ho fetisisa lapeng la hao selemo le selemo?
body.backTranslation: Think about the seed you buy again and again. Which repeated seed purchase eats the most money in your household every year?

body.text: Kgetha sejalo se le seng lethathamong la hao la ho lema. E etse qalo ya hao e sebetsang ya ho boloka peo. O se ke wa leka ho boloka tsohle hang-hang.
body.backTranslation: Choose one crop on your planting list. Make it your working start to saving seed. Do not try to save everything at once.

english.heading: Learning Outcomes
body: This lesson ends with a working seed store, not a list of facts.
You will make four decisions.
What will you save?
How will you process it?
How will you protect it?
And how will you know it is still alive before you depend on it?
Which of these four decisions is least familiar to you?
Say them again in your own words: select, process, protect and verify.

heading.text: Seo O Tla Ithuta Sona

body.text: Thuto ena e qetella ka polokelo ya peo e sebetsang, e seng lethathamo la dintlha.
body.backTranslation: This lesson ends with a working seed store, not a list of facts.

body.text: O tla etsa diqeto tse nne.
body.backTranslation: You will make four decisions.

body.text: O tla boloka eng?
body.backTranslation: What will you save?

body.text: O tla e lokisa jwang?
body.backTranslation: How will you prepare it?

body.text: O tla e sireletsa jwang?
body.backTranslation: How will you protect it?

body.text: Mme o tla tseba jwang hore e ntse e phela pele o itshetleha ka yona?
body.backTranslation: And how will you know that it is still alive before you rely on it?

body.text: Ke efe ya diqeto tsena tse nne eo o e tlwaetseng hanyane ka ho fetisisa?
body.backTranslation: Which of these four decisions are you least used to?

body.text: Di phete ka mantswe a hao: kgetha, lokisa, sireletsa, mme o netefatse.
body.backTranslation: Repeat them in your own words: choose, prepare, protect, and confirm.

english.heading: Open-Pollinated Seed and F1 Seed
body: Open-pollinated seed is not magic.
A stable variety can produce similar generations when it is properly isolated or self-pollinated.
F1 seed usually remains alive. But the next generation separates into different combinations of the parent traits.
The problem is unpredictability, not failure to germinate.
Think about one small bed on your own plot. Why could unpredictable plants be a risk when space is limited?
If you have seed packets, check whether they are marked open-pollinated or F1. Which would you choose for saving dependable seed?
Remember: the next F1 generation varies. It does not automatically die.

heading.text: Peo ya Open-Pollinated le Peo ya F1

body.text: Peo ya open-pollinated ha se mohlolo.
body.backTranslation: Open-pollinated seed is not a miracle.

body.text: Stable variety e ka hlahisa meloko e tshwanang ha e arotswe hantle kapa ha e etsa self-pollination.
body.backTranslation: A stable variety can produce generations that are alike when it is separated well or when it does self-pollination.

body.text: Peo ya F1 hangata e ntse e phela. Empa moloko o latelang o arohana ka metswako e fapaneng ya dipharologanyo tsa batswadi.
body.backTranslation: F1 seed is usually still alive. But the next generation splits into different mixtures of the parents' differences.

body.text: Bothata ke hore ha ho tsejwe esale pele hore dimela di tla ba jwang, e seng ho hloleha ho mela.
body.backTranslation: The problem is that it is not known beforehand what the plants will be like, not a failure to germinate.

body.text: Nahana ka bethe e nyane e le nngwe ya serapa tshimong ya hao. Ke hobaneng dimela tse sa tsejweng esale pele di ka ba kotsi ha sebaka se lekanyeditswe?
body.backTranslation: Think of one small garden bed in your field. Why could plants that are not known beforehand be a risk when space is limited?

body.text: Haeba o na le dipakete tsa peo, hlahloba hore na di tshwailwe open-pollinated kapa F1. Ke efe eo o ka e kgethang ho boloka peo e tshepehang?
body.backTranslation: If you have seed packets, check whether they are marked open-pollinated or F1. Which one could you choose to save reliable seed?

body.text: Hopola: moloko o latelang wa F1 o a fapana. Ha o shwe ka boyona.
body.backTranslation: Remember: the next generation of F1 is different. It does not die by itself.

english.heading: Watch: Open-Pollinated Seed and F1 Seed
body: Watch both sides.
Both kinds of seed germinate.
Open-pollinated seed produces similar plants when the variety is stable and pollination is properly managed.
Seed saved from an F1 plant also germinates. But its next generation varies. Some plants may be tall. Others may be short. Their vigour and yield may differ.
Ask yourself what this means when choosing seed to save.
If you understand the difference, you can explain it in one sentence: both germinate, but the next F1 generation is unpredictable.

heading.text: Sheba: Peo ya Open-Pollinated le Peo ya F1
heading.backTranslation: Look: Open-Pollinated Seed and F1 Seed

body.text: Sheba mahlakore ka bobedi.
body.backTranslation: Look at both sides.

body.text: Mefuta ka bobedi ya peo e a mela.
body.backTranslation: Both kinds of seed germinate.

body.text: Peo ya open-pollinated e hlahisa dimela tse tshwanang ha e le stable variety mme pollination e laolwa hantle.
body.backTranslation: Open-pollinated seed produces plants that are alike when it is a stable variety and pollination is controlled well.

body.text: Peo e bolokilweng ho semela sa F1 le yona e a mela. Empa moloko wa yona o latelang o a fapana. Dimela tse ding di ka ba telele. Tse ding di ka ba kgutshwane. Matla a tsona a kgolo le tlhahiso ya tsona di ka fapana.
body.backTranslation: Seed saved from an F1 plant also germinates. But its next generation differs. Some plants may be tall. Others may be short. Their vigour and their yield may differ.

body.text: Ipotse hore na sena se bolela eng ha o kgetha peo eo o tla e boloka.
body.backTranslation: Ask yourself what this means when you choose seed that you will save.

body.text: Haeba o utlwisisa phapang, o ka e hlalosa ka polelo e le nngwe: mefuta ka bobedi e a mela, empa moloko o latelang wa F1 ha o tsejwe esale pele.
body.backTranslation: If you understand the difference, you can explain it in one sentence: both kinds germinate, but the next generation of F1 is not known beforehand.

english.heading: Seed Sovereignty
body: Seed sovereignty does not live in a slogan.
It lives in a dry packet, a written record and knowledge of how the seed behaves.
Your household begins it. Neighbours extend it. The seasons make the local seed collection more useful.
Which seed does your household already save best?
Draw a small map of the homes near you. Beside each home, write one crop that household could bring to a seed exchange.
Sovereignty needs three things: usable seed, written information and exchange.

heading.text: Boikemelo ba Peo (seed sovereignty)

body.text: Boikemelo ba peo ha bo phele mohoong (slogan).
body.backTranslation: Seed self-reliance does not live in a slogan (slogan).

body.text: Bo phela paketeng e omileng, tlalehong e ngotsweng le tsebong ya hore peo e itshwara jwang.
body.backTranslation: It lives in a dry packet, in written records and in knowing how the seed behaves.

body.text: Lelapa la heno le qala sena. Baahisani ba se atolosa. Dinako tsa selemo di etsa hore pokello ya peo ya sebakeng seo e be le thuso e ngata ho feta.
body.backTranslation: Your household starts this. Neighbours spread it. The seasons of the year make a local seed collection more useful.

body.text: Ke peo efe eo lelapa la heno le seng le e boloka hantle ka ho fetisisa?
body.backTranslation: Which seed does your household already save best?

body.text: Taka mmapa o monyane wa matlo a haufi le wena. Haufi le ntlo e nngwe le e nngwe, ngola sejalo se le seng seo lelapa leo le ka se tlisang phapanyetsanong ya peo.
body.backTranslation: Draw a small map of the houses near you. Near each house, write one crop that that household could bring to a seed swap.

body.text: Boikemelo bo hloka dintho tse tharo: peo e ka sebediswang, tlhahisoleseding e ngotsweng le phapanyetsano.
body.backTranslation: Self-reliance needs three things: usable seed, written information and swapping.

english.heading: Watch: Household Seed Network
body: Well-saved seed becomes more powerful when it is known and shared.
Watch one household begin by saving seed well from one crop. Dry seed goes into clean packets. Some packets move to neighbouring homes. The neighbours share different seed in return.
By the end, each household holds more varieties than it had before.
Think about which seed you could share and which seed you might receive from a neighbour. Seed moves. Knowledge and trust must move with it.

heading.text: Sheba: Marangrang a Peo a Malapa

body.text: Peo e bolokilweng hantle e ba le matla le ho feta ha e tsejwa mme e arolelwa.
body.backTranslation: Well-saved seed becomes even stronger when it is known and shared.

body.text: Sheba lelapa le le leng le qala ka ho boloka peo hantle ho sejalo se le seng. Peo e omileng e kena dipaketeng tse hlwekileng. Dipakete tse ding di ya malapeng a baahisani. Baahisani ba arolelana peo e fapaneng ka phapanyetsano.
body.backTranslation: Look at one household starting by saving seed well from one crop. Dry seed goes into clean packets. Other packets go to the neighbours' households. Neighbours share different seed through swapping.

body.text: Qetellong, lelapa le le leng le le leng le na le mefuta e mengata ya peo (varieties) ho feta eo le neng le e na le yona pele.
body.backTranslation: In the end, each household has more varieties (varieties) of seed than it had before.

body.text: Nahana ka peo eo o ka e arolelanang le eo o ka e fumanang ho moahisani. Peo e a tsamaya. Tsebo le tshepo di tshwanetse ho tsamaya le yona.
body.backTranslation: Think about the seed you could share and what you could get from a neighbour. Seed travels. Knowledge and trust must travel with it.

english.heading: Select Several Parent Plants
body: The largest fruit is not always the best seed parent.
Look at the whole plant.
Was it healthy?
Did it mature at the right time?
Was it true to type?
Save from several good plants, especially in cross-pollinated crops. This prevents the next generation from coming from only one parent.
What would make you reject a seed plant even if its fruit were large?
Go to your own plot. Point out the plants you would select and the plants you would reject. Choose several healthy, true-to-type plants. Reject diseased plants and those that are not true to type.

heading.text: Kgetha Dimela tse Mmalwa tsa Motswadi

body.text: Tholwana e kgolo ka ho fetisisa ha se kamehla e leng motswadi o molemo ka ho fetisisa wa peo.
body.backTranslation: The biggest fruit is not always the best seed parent.

body.text: Sheba semela sohle.
body.backTranslation: Look at the whole plant.

body.text: Na se ne se phetse hantle?
body.backTranslation: Was it healthy?

body.text: Na se ile sa butswa ka nako e loketseng?
body.backTranslation: Did it ripen at the right time?

body.text: Na se ne se tshwana le mofuta wa sona (true to type)?
body.backTranslation: Was it like its variety (true to type)?

body.text: Boloka peo ho dimela tse mmalwa tse ntle, haholoholo dijalong tsa cross-pollinated. Sena se thibela moloko o latelang hore o se tswe ho motswadi a le mong feela.
body.backTranslation: Save seed from several good plants, especially in cross-pollinated crops. This prevents the next generation from coming from only one parent.

body.text: Ke eng e neng e ka etsa hore o hane semela sa peo, leha tholwana ya sona e ne e le kgolo?
body.backTranslation: What would make you reject a seed plant, even if its fruit was big?

body.text: Eya tshimong ya hao. Supa dimela tseo o ka di kgethang le tseo o ka di hanang. Kgetha dimela tse mmalwa tse phetseng hantle tse tshwanang le mofuta wa tsona. Hana dimela tse nang le malwetse le tse sa tshwaneng le mofuta wa tsona.
body.backTranslation: Go to your field. Point out the plants you could choose and those you could reject. Choose several healthy plants that are like their variety. Reject plants that have diseases and those that are not like their variety.

english.heading: Control Pollination
body: Some crops mostly self-pollinate. A small garden can therefore keep the variety similar.
Crops pollinated by wind or insects can cross over long distances.
The distance needed depends on the crop, the place and the purpose of the seed. Do not promise varietal purity until you have checked the crop.
How can you separate two varieties without using distance?
You can plant them at different times so they do not flower together. You can also control pollination by hand or with covers.
Remember the three tools: distance, flowering time or controlled pollination.

heading.text: Laola Pollination

body.text: Dijalo tse ding hangata di etsa self-pollination. Ka hona serapa se senyane se ka boloka mofuta (variety) o tshwana.
body.backTranslation: Some crops usually do self-pollination. Therefore a small garden can keep a variety (variety) that is the same.

body.text: Dijalo tseo pollen ya tsona e tsamaiswang ke moya kapa dikokwanyana di ka tswakana (cross) ho pholletsa le sebaka se selelele.
body.backTranslation: Crops whose pollen is carried by wind or insects can mix (cross) across a long space.

body.text: Bohole bo hlokehang bo ya ka sejalo, sebaka le morero wa peo. O se ke wa kholofetsa bohlweke ba mofuta (variety) ho fihlela o hlahlobile sejalo.
body.backTranslation: The distance needed depends on the crop, the place and the purpose of the seed. Do not promise the purity of a variety (variety) until you have checked the crop.

body.text: O ka aroganya mefuta e mmedi (varieties) jwang ntle le ho sebedisa sebaka?
body.backTranslation: How can you separate two varieties (varieties) without using distance?

body.text: O ka di jala ka dinako tse fapaneng hore di se ke tsa thunya mmoho. O ka boela wa laola pollination ka letsoho kapa ka dikwahelo (covers).
body.backTranslation: You can plant them at different times so that they do not flower together. You can also control pollination by hand or with coverings (covers).

body.text: Hopola disebediswa tse tharo: sebaka, nako ya ho thunya kapa pollination e laolwang.
body.backTranslation: Remember three tools: space, time of flowering, or controlled pollination.

english.heading: Watch: Self-Pollination and Crossing
body: Follow the path of the pollen.
In self-pollination, pollen moves within one flower from the part that produces it to the part that receives it. This often helps the variety remain similar.
In a maize field, wind carries pollen from the tassels to the silks. If two varieties are close together and flower at the same time, they can cross.
Think about how distance or different flowering times could prevent that on your own plot.

heading.text: Sheba: Self-Pollination le Ho Tswakana (crossing)
heading.backTranslation: Look: Self-Pollination and To Mix with One Another (crossing)

body.text: Latela tsela ya pollen.
body.backTranslation: Follow the path of pollen.

body.text: Nakong ya self-pollination, pollen e tsamaya ka hare ho palesa e le nngwe ho tloha karolong e e hlahisang ho ya karolong e e amohelang. Sena hangata se thusa hore mofuta (variety) o tswele pele o tshwana.
body.backTranslation: At the time of self-pollination, pollen moves inside one flower from the part that produces [it] to the part that receives [it]. This usually helps the variety (variety) to continue being the same.

body.text: Tshimong ya poone, moya o jara pollen ho tloha ho tassels ho ya ho silks. Haeba mefuta e mmedi (varieties) e haufi mme e thunya ka nako e le nngwe, e ka tswakana (cross).
body.backTranslation: In a field of maize, wind carries pollen from tassels to silks. If two varieties (varieties) are near and flower at one time, they can mix (cross).

body.text: Nahana hore sebaka kapa dinako tse fapaneng tsa ho thunya di ka thibela seo jwang tshimong ya hao.
body.backTranslation: Think about how distance or different flowering times could prevent that in your field.

english.heading: Dry and Wet Processing
body: There are two broad ways to process seed.
Dry seed matures in a pod, head or cob. It is collected when fully mature.
Seed inside a fleshy fruit must first be separated from the flesh.
Brief fermentation is especially useful for tomato seed. It is not a rule for every wet-seeded crop.
Think about the crops in your area. Which fit the dry method? Which fit the wet method?
If you have seed or fruit nearby, sort the examples into these two types. Explain the difference by describing what the seed is like at harvest.

heading.text: Ho Lokisa Peo ka Mokgwa o Omileng le o Metsi
heading.backTranslation: Preparing Seed by the Dry and Wet Method

body.text: Ho na le ditsela tse pedi tse kgolo tsa ho lokisa peo.
body.backTranslation: There are two big ways of preparing seed.

body.text: Peo e omileng e butswa ka hare ho pod, hlooho kapa cob. E bokelwa ha e butsitse ka ho feletseng.
body.backTranslation: Dry seed ripens inside the pod, head or cob. It is collected when it is completely ripe.

body.text: Peo e ka hare ho tholwana e nang le nama e tlameha pele ho aroswa le nama.
body.backTranslation: Seed inside a fleshy fruit must first be separated from the flesh.

body.text: Ho etsa fermentation e kgutshwane ho thusa haholoholo ho peo ya tamati. Ha se molao bakeng sa dijalo tsohle tse nang le peo e metsi.
body.backTranslation: A short fermentation especially helps with tomato seed. It is not a rule for all crops with wet seed.

body.text: Nahana ka dijalo tsa sebaka sa heno. Ke dife tse tshwanelang mokgwa o omileng? Ke dife tse tshwanelang mokgwa o metsi?
body.backTranslation: Think about the crops of your area. Which suit the dry method? Which suit the wet method?

body.text: Haeba o na le peo kapa ditholwana haufi, aroganya mehlala ka mefuta ena e mmedi. Hlalosa phapang ka ho hlalosa hore peo e jwang nakong ya kotulo.
body.backTranslation: If you have seed or fruits nearby, separate examples into these two kinds. Explain the difference by describing how the seed is at harvest time.

english.heading: Process Dry Seed
body: Leave dry-seeded crops on the plant until the seed is fully mature.
Collect it before weather, birds or bursting pods take the harvest.
Remove chaff and damaged seed.
Then spread the clean seed in a single layer in moving air and shade.
What tells you that dry seed is mature enough to collect?
If you have a dry pod or seed head, handle it. Listen for the seed. Compare green, flexible plant material with brown, brittle material.
Wait for maturity. For final drying, use shade and airflow.

heading.text: Lokisa Peo e Omileng

body.text: Tlogela dijalo tse nang le peo e omileng semeleng ho fihlela peo e butsitse ka ho feletseng.
body.backTranslation: Leave crops with dry seed on the plant until the seed is completely ripe.

body.text: E bokele pele boemo ba lehodimo, dinonyana kapa dipod tse phatlohang di nka kotulo.
body.backTranslation: Collect it before weather, birds or bursting pods take the harvest.

body.text: Tlosa makgapetla (chaff) le peo e senyehileng.
body.backTranslation: Remove the husks (chaff) and the damaged seed.

body.text: Jwale phatlalatsa peo e hlwekileng ka lera le le leng moyeng o tsamayang le moriting.
body.backTranslation: Now spread the clean seed in a single layer in moving air and in shade.

body.text: Ke eng e o bolellang hore peo e omileng e butsitse ho lekana ho bokelwa?
body.backTranslation: What tells you that dry seed is ripe enough to be collected?

body.text: Haeba o na le pod kapa hlooho ya peo e omileng, e tshware. Mamela peo. Bapisa thepa ya semela e tala e kobehang habonolo le e sootho e robehang habonolo.
body.backTranslation: If you have a pod or head of dry seed, hold it. Listen to the seed. Compare the material of a green plant that bends easily with a brown one that breaks easily.

body.text: Emela hore peo e butswe. Bakeng sa ho omisa qetellong, sebedisa moriti le moya o tsamayang.
body.backTranslation: Wait for the seed to ripen. For the final drying, use shade and moving air.

english.heading: Watch: Dry Processing
body: Allow the seed to mature on the plant before collecting it.
Watch how it is collected once mature. Chaff and debris are removed. Damaged seed is taken out.
The clean seed is then spread in a single layer in moving air and shade.
Follow the steps in order: mature, collect, clean, dry.
Think about where you could carry out each part of this process.

heading.text: Sheba: Mokgwa o Omileng (dry processing)

body.text: Dumella peo hore e butswe semeleng pele e bokellwa.
body.backTranslation: Allow the seed to ripen on the plant before it is collected.

body.text: Sheba kamoo e bokellwang ka teng hang ha e butswe. Makgapetla (chaff) le ditshila di tloswa. Peo e senyehileng e ntshiwa.
body.backTranslation: Look at how it is collected once it is ripe. Husks (chaff) and dirt are removed. Damaged seed is taken out.

body.text: Peo e hlwekileng e anngwa ka lera le le leng moyeng o tsamayang le moriting.
body.backTranslation: Clean seed is spread in a single layer in moving air and in shade.

body.text: Latela mehato ka tatellano: butswa, bokella, hlwekisa, omisa.
body.backTranslation: Follow the steps in order: ripen, collect, clean, dry.

body.text: Nahana hore na o ka etsa karolo ka nngwe ya tshebetso ena kae.
body.backTranslation: Think about where you could do each part of this process.

english.heading: Wet Processing for Tomato Seed
body: Scoop tomato seed and flesh into a clean jar with a little water.
Leave it open or loosely covered. Keep it out of direct sun.
After two to three days, a light film and a sour smell may appear.
Rinse promptly. Remove debris. Then spread the clean seed thinly to dry.
Do not seal an actively fermenting jar.
Think about the signs that tell you the process has begun. Also think about signs that would make you discard the batch.
Find a jar, a sieve and a drying plate. When you are ready, start a small batch. Remember the order: scoop, ferment briefly, rinse and dry completely.

heading.text: Mokgwa o Metsi (wet processing): Peo ya Tamati
heading.backTranslation: The Wet Method (wet processing): Tomato Seed

body.text: Kenya peo ya tamati le nama ya yona ka jareng e hlwekileng e nang le metsi a mannyane.
body.backTranslation: Put the tomato seed and its flesh in a clean jar with a little water.

body.text: E tlohele e bulehile kapa e kwahetswe ka tsela e sa tiyang. E boloke kantle ho letsatsi le tobileng.
body.backTranslation: Leave it open or loosely covered. Keep it out of direct sun.

body.text: Kamora matsatsi a mabedi ho isa ho a mararo, lera le bobebe le monko o bodila di ka hlaha.
body.backTranslation: After two to three days, a light layer and a sour smell may appear.

body.text: Hlatswa kapele. Tlosa ditshila. Ebe o anya peo e hlwekileng e tshesaane hore e ome.
body.backTranslation: Wash quickly. Remove the dirt. Then spread the clean seed thinly to dry.

body.text: O se ke wa kwala jara e ntseng e fermenta.
body.backTranslation: Do not close a jar that is still fermenting.

body.text: Nahana ka matshwao a o bolellang hore tshebetso e qadile. Hape nahana ka matshwao a ka o etsang hore o lahle sehlopha seo.
body.backTranslation: Think about the signs that tell you the process has started. Also think about the signs that could make you throw that batch away.

body.text: Fumana jara, sefe le poleiti ya ho omisa. Ha o se o itokiseditse, qala sehlopha se senyenyane. Hopola tatellano: ntsha, fermenta nakwana, hlatswa o be o omise ka ho feletseng.
body.backTranslation: Find a jar, a sieve and a plate for drying. When you are ready, start a small batch. Remember the order: take out, ferment briefly, wash and then dry completely.

english.heading: Watch: Wet Processing for Tomato Seed
body: Watch the whole process in order.
A ripe tomato is opened. The seed and gel are scooped into a clean jar. Only a little water is added.
The jar is left open or loosely covered for two to three days.
When a light film and sour smell appear, the contents are poured through a sieve. The seed is rinsed until it is clean.
Finally, the seed is spread in a single layer in the shade until completely dry.
Repeat the steps to yourself: scoop, ferment briefly, rinse, dry completely.

heading.text: Sheba: Mokgwa o Metsi bakeng sa Peo ya Tamati
heading.backTranslation: Look: The Wet Method for Tomato Seed

body.text: Sheba tshebetso yohle ka tatellano.
body.backTranslation: Look at the whole process in order.

body.text: Tamati e butsweng e a bulwa. Peo le jele di kenngwa ka jareng e hlwekileng. Ho kenngwa metsi a mannyane feela.
body.backTranslation: A ripe tomato is opened. The seed and the jelly are put into a clean jar. Only a little water is added.

body.text: Jara e tlohelwa e bulehile kapa e kwahetswe ka tsela e sa tiyang ka matsatsi a mabedi ho isa ho a mararo.
body.backTranslation: The jar is left open or loosely covered for two to three days.

body.text: Ha lera le bobebe le monko o bodila di hlaha, dikahare di tshollelwa ka sefeng. Peo e hlatsuwa ho fihlela e hlweka.
body.backTranslation: When a light layer and a sour smell appear, the contents are poured into a sieve. The seed is washed until it is clean.

body.text: Qetellong, peo e anngwa ka lera le le leng moriting ho fihlela e omme ka ho feletseng.
body.backTranslation: Finally, the seed is spread in a single layer in shade until it is completely dry.

body.text: Ipolelle mehato: ntsha, fermenta nakwana, hlatswa, omisa ka ho feletseng.
body.backTranslation: Say the steps to yourself: take out, ferment briefly, wash, dry completely.

english.heading: Practical Activity
body: This is where the lesson leaves the screen and reaches your hands.
Start one real batch of wet-processed seed.
Use one ripe, healthy fruit, a clean jar, a spoon, a little water, a sieve and a drying plate.
Put the seed, flesh and a little water into the jar. Add a label with the date.
You will look after this jar after the lesson. Decide now when you will inspect it, when you will rinse it and when you will dry the seed.
Your jar needs a date and a return plan. Write down the date when you will inspect it after two days.

heading.text: Mosebetsi wa ho Etsa

body.text: Mona ke moo thuto e tlohang skrineng e fihlang diatleng tsa hao.
body.backTranslation: This is where the lesson leaves the screen and reaches your hands.

body.text: Qala sehlopha se le seng sa 'nnete' sa peo e sebetsitsweng ka wet processing.
body.backTranslation: Start one 'real' batch of seed processed by wet processing.

body.text: Sebedisa tholwana e le nngwe e butsweng e phetseng hantle, jara e hlwekileng, kgaba (spoon), metsi a mannyane, sefe le poleiti ya ho omisa.
body.backTranslation: Use one healthy ripe fruit, a clean jar, a spoon (spoon), a little water, a sieve and a plate for drying.

body.text: Kenya peo, nama le metsi a mannyane ka jareng. Kgomaretsa leibole e nang le letsatsi la kgwedi (date).
body.backTranslation: Put the seed, flesh and a little water in a jar. Stick on a label with the date of the month (date).

body.text: O tla hlokomela jara ena kamora thuto. Etsa qeto hona jwale hore na o tla e hlahloba neng, o tla e hlatswa neng le hore o tla omisa peo neng.
body.backTranslation: You will look after this jar after the lesson. Decide now when you will check it, when you will wash it and when you will dry the seed.

body.text: Jara ya hao e hloka letsatsi la kgwedi (date) le moralo wa ho kgutla. Ngola letsatsi leo o tla e hlahloba ka lona kamora matsatsi a mabedi.
body.backTranslation: Your jar needs a date (date) and a plan for coming back. Write the day on which you will check it after two days.

english.heading: Dry First, Seal Later
body: Drying is not a decorative final step.
Moist seed keeps breathing. It can heat, rot or die in storage.
Use shade, moving air and time.
Seal seed only when you are sure it is dry.
Which place in your home has shade and airflow, but is protected from rain and cooking steam?
Choose one safe drying place. Then identify one unsafe place.
Repeat this to check your understanding: dry first, seal later.

heading.text: Omisa Pele, Kwala Hamorao

body.text: Ho omisa hase mohato o kgabisang wa ho qetela.
body.backTranslation: Drying is not a decorative last step.

body.text: Peo e metsi e ntse e phefumoloha. E ka futhumala, ya bola kapa ya shwa ha e bolokilwe.
body.backTranslation: Wet seed is still breathing. It can heat up, rot or die when stored.

body.text: Sebedisa moriti, moya o tsamayang le nako.
body.backTranslation: Use shade, moving air and time.

body.text: Kwala peo feela ha o tseba hantle hore e omme.
body.backTranslation: Close up seed only when you know well that it is dry.

body.text: Ke sebaka sefe ka lapeng la hao se nang le moriti le moya, empa se sireletsehileng pula le mouwane wa ho pheha?
body.backTranslation: Which place in your home has shade and air, but is protected from rain and cooking steam?

body.text: Kgetha sebaka se le seng se bolokehileng sa ho omisa. Ebe o bona sebaka se le seng se sa bolokehang.
body.backTranslation: Choose one safe place for drying. Then find one place that is not safe.

body.text: Pheta sena ho hlahloba kutlwisiso ya hao: omisa pele, kwala hamorao.
body.backTranslation: Repeat this to check your understanding: dry first, close later.

english.heading: Protect Seed from Heat, Light and Moisture
body: Paper packets breathe and organise seed. But they are not enough in a humid climate.
Once the seed is completely dry, place the labelled packets inside a sealed, moisture-proof container. If available, include a food-safe desiccant.
Keep the container as cool and dark as possible in your home.
Which room or cupboard in your home stays coolest and driest?
Compare a paper envelope on its own with an envelope inside a sealed container.
Safe storage has two layers: a labelled paper packet inside a dry, sealed container.

heading.text: Sireletsa Peo ho Motjheso, Lesedi le Mongobo
heading.backTranslation: Protect Seed from Heat, Light and Moisture

body.text: Dipakete tsa pampiri di a phefumoloha mme di hlophisa peo. Empa ha di lekane boemong ba maemo a mongobo o mongata.
body.backTranslation: Paper packets breathe and organise the seed. But they are not enough in conditions of a lot of moisture.

body.text: Hang ha peo e omme ka ho feletseng, kenya dipakete tse nang le dileibole ka setshelong se kwetsweng, se thibelang mongobo. Haeba e fumaneha, kenya food-safe desiccant.
body.backTranslation: Once the seed is completely dry, put the packets with labels in a closed container that keeps out moisture. If it is available, add a food-safe desiccant.

body.text: Boloka setshelo se phodile le se lefifi kamoo ho ka kgonehang ka lapeng la hao.
body.backTranslation: Keep the container as cool and dark as possible in your home.

body.text: Ke kamore efe kapa kabinete efe ka lapeng la hao e dulang e phodile ebile e omme ho fetisisa?
body.backTranslation: Which room or cabinet in your home stays the coolest and driest?

body.text: Bapisa enfelopo ya pampiri e se nang setshelo le enfelopo e ka hare ho setshelo se kwetsweng.
body.backTranslation: Compare a paper envelope with no container and an envelope inside a closed container.

body.text: Polokelo e bolokehileng e na le dikarolo tse pedi: pakete ya pampiri e nang le leibole ka hare ho setshelo se omileng, se kwetsweng.
body.backTranslation: Safe storage has two parts: a paper packet with a label inside a dry, closed container.

english.heading: Label Every Packet
body: Storage protects the seed physically. Written information protects its meaning.
The packet must tell the next person what crop it is.
It must give the variety or local name.
It must say when the seed was saved and where it came from.
Which local names could be lost if you write only the crop name?
Take a blank packet. Practise writing the four pieces of information: crop, variety or local name, date and source.
Check again that all four are present.

heading.text: Beha Leibole Paketeng Ka Nngwe
heading.backTranslation: Put a Label on Each Packet

body.text: Polokelo e sireletsa peo ka mmele. Tlhahisoleseding e ngotsweng e sireletsa moelelo wa yona.
body.backTranslation: Storage protects the seed physically. Written information protects its meaning.

body.text: Pakete e tlameha ho bolella motho ya latelang hore ke sejalo sefe.
body.backTranslation: A packet must tell the next person which crop it is.

body.text: E tlameha ho fana ka lebitso la mofuta (variety) kapa lebitso la lehae.
body.backTranslation: It must give the name of the variety (variety) or the local name.

body.text: E tlameha ho bolela hore peo e bolokilwe neng le hore e tswa kae.
body.backTranslation: It must say when the seed was stored and where it comes from.

body.text: Ke mabitso afe a lehae a ka lahlehang ha o ngola lebitso la sejalo feela?
body.backTranslation: Which local names could be lost if you write only the name of the crop?

body.text: Nka pakete e se nang letho. Ikwetlise ho ngola dintlha tse nne: sejalo, mofuta (variety) kapa lebitso la lehae, letsatsi la kgwedi le mohlodi.
body.backTranslation: Take an empty packet. Practise writing four things: the crop, the variety (variety) or local name, the date and the source.

body.text: Hlahloba hape hore tse nne kaofela di teng.
body.backTranslation: Check again that all four are there.

english.heading: Ten-Seed Germination Test
body: A seed packet can look perfect even when the seed is losing life.
Ten seeds make the calculation easy.
Keep them warm and moist. Do not submerge them in water.
Then count the normal seedlings.
Six out of ten is about sixty percent. That tells you to sow more heavily, use the seed only as a trial, or replace it.
If eight seeds out of ten germinate, what percentage is that?
The answer is eighty percent.
Start a ten-seed test with an old packet. Write down the date and the day when you will count.

heading.text: Germination Test ya Dipeo tse Leshome

body.text: Pakete ya peo e ka bonahala e se na sekoli le ha peo e ntse e lahlehelwa ke bophelo.
body.backTranslation: A packet of seed may appear to have no fault even though the seed is still losing life.

body.text: Dipeo tse leshome di etsa hore palo e be bonolo.
body.backTranslation: Ten seeds make the counting easy.

body.text: Di boloke di futhumetse ebile di metsi. O se ke wa di qwedisa ka metsing.
body.backTranslation: Keep them warm and moist. Do not drown them in water.

body.text: Ebe o bala dimela tse nyane (seedlings) tse tlwaelehileng.
body.backTranslation: Then count the normal seedlings (seedlings).

body.text: Tse tsheletseng ho tse leshome ke hoo e ka bang diperesente tse mashome a tsheletseng. Seo se o bolella hore o jale ka botenya bo fetang, o sebedise peo e le teko feela, kapa o e nkele sebaka ka peo e nngwe.
body.backTranslation: Six out of ten is about sixty percent. That tells you to sow more thickly, use the seed only as a trial, or replace it with other seed.

body.text: Haeba dipeo tse robedi ho tse leshome di mela, ke diperesente tse kae?
body.backTranslation: If eight seeds out of ten germinate, what percentage is that?

body.text: Karabo ke diperesente tse mashome a robedi.
body.backTranslation: The answer is eighty percent.

body.text: Qala teko ya dipeo tse leshome ka pakete ya kgale. Ngola letsatsi la kgwedi le letsatsi leo o tla bala ka lona.
body.backTranslation: Start a ten-seed test with an old packet. Write the date and the day on which you will count.

english.heading: Watch: Ten-Seed Germination Test
body: Count exactly ten seeds.
Place them in two rows of five.
Keep them on moist paper or cloth. Do not submerge them in water.
After some time, count again.
Here, six have germinated. Four have not. The total is still ten.
The germination rate is therefore sixty percent.
Check yourself. Did you count ten at the start, six germinated seeds and four ungerminated seeds at the end?

heading.text: Sheba: Germination Test ya Dipeo tse Leshome
heading.backTranslation: Look: Germination Test of Ten Seeds

body.text: Bala dipeo tse leshome ka nepo.
body.backTranslation: Count ten seeds accurately.

body.text: Di behe ka mela e mebedi ya tse hlano.
body.backTranslation: Place them in two rows of five.

body.text: Di boloke hodima pampiri kapa lesela le nang le mongobo. O se ke wa di qwedisa ka metsing.
body.backTranslation: Keep them on damp paper or cloth. Do not drown them in water.

body.text: Kamora nakwana, bala hape.
body.backTranslation: After a short while, count again.

body.text: Mona, tse tsheletseng di mehile. Tse nne ha di a mela. Palo kaofela e ntse e le leshome.
body.backTranslation: Here, six have sprouted. Four have not germinated. The total is still ten.

body.text: Kahoo sekgahla sa germination ke diperesente tse mashome a tsheletseng.
body.backTranslation: So the germination rate is sixty percent.

body.text: Itlhahlobe. Na o ile wa bala dipeo tse leshome qalong, dipeo tse tsheletseng tse mehileng le dipeo tse nne tse sa meleng qetellong?
body.backTranslation: Check yourself. Did you count ten seeds at the start, six sprouted seeds and four seeds that did not germinate at the end?

english.heading: Share Seed with Its Information
body: A seed exchange is not a table of unknown packets.
A good exchange moves information with the seed.
It tells you what the seed is. Where it came from. When it was saved. And whether it has been tested.
This honesty strengthens the whole network.
What information would help you trust seed from another household?
Take one of your packets. Practise describing it before sharing it. Give the seed and its basic history together.

heading.text: Arolelana Peo le Tlhahisoleseding ya Yona

body.text: Phapanyetsano ya peo hase tafole ya dipakete tse sa tsejweng.
body.backTranslation: A seed swap is not a table of unknown packets.

body.text: Phapanyetsano e ntle ya peo e tsamaisa tlhahisoleseding hammoho le peo.
body.backTranslation: A good seed swap moves information together with the seed.

body.text: E o bolella hore peo ke eng. E tswa kae. E bolokilwe neng. Mme na e se e lekotswe.
body.backTranslation: It tells you what the seed is. Where it comes from. When it was stored. And whether it has been tested.

body.text: Botshepehi bona bo matlafatsa marangrang kaofela.
body.backTranslation: This trustworthiness strengthens the whole network.

body.text: Ke tlhahisoleseding efe e ka o thusang ho tshepa peo e tswang lelapeng le leng?
body.backTranslation: What information could help you trust seed that comes from another household?

body.text: Nka e nngwe ya dipakete tsa hao. Ikwetlise ho e hlalosa pele o e arolelana. Fana ka peo le nalane ya yona ya motheo hammoho.
body.backTranslation: Take one of your packets. Practise describing it before you share it. Give the seed and its basic history together.

english.heading: Field Assignment
body: This task is small enough to finish. It is important enough to matter.
Build one working seed-storage container.
Put labelled paper packets inside a dry, sealed container.
Take a photograph of it.
Then name the crop whose seed you will save this season.
The photograph is evidence. The packet is a beginning.
What do you still need to finish this at home?
Write a short materials list. Choose a completion date.

Before sealing the container, check your work: the seed is completely dry; every packet has the crop, variety and date; the container is cool, dark and protected from moisture; and you selected several healthy parent plants.

heading.text: Mosebetsi wa Tshimong

body.text: Mosebetsi ona o monyane, o ka o phetha. O bohlokwa ka ho lekana hore o etse phapang.
body.backTranslation: This task is small, you can finish it. It is equally important in making a difference.

body.text: Aha setshelo se le seng se sebetsang sa polokelo ya peo.
body.backTranslation: Build one working seed storage container.

body.text: Kenya dipakete tsa pampiri tse nang le dileibole ka setshelong se omileng, se kwetsweng.
body.backTranslation: Put paper packets with labels in a dry, closed container.

body.text: Nka setshwantsho sa sona.
body.backTranslation: Take a picture of it.

body.text: Ebe o reha sejalo seo o tla boloka peo ya sona sehla sena.
body.backTranslation: Then name the crop whose seed you will save this season.

body.text: Setshwantsho ke bopaki. Pakete ke qalo.
body.backTranslation: The picture is proof. The packet is the beginning.

body.text: Ke eng eo o ntseng o e hloka ho phetha sena lapeng?
body.backTranslation: What do you still need to finish this at home?

body.text: Ngola lethathamo le lekgutshwane la thepa. Kgetha letsatsi la ho qeta.
body.backTranslation: Write a short list of materials. Choose a day to finish.

body.text: Pele o kwala setshelo, hlahloba mosebetsi: peo e omme ka ho feletseng; pakete ka nngwe e na le sejalo, mofuta (variety) le letsatsi la kgwedi; setshelo se phodile, se lefifi mme se sireletsehile mongobong; mme o kgethile dimela tse mmalwa tsa batswadi tse phetseng hantle.
body.backTranslation: Before you close the container, check the work: the seed is completely dry; each packet has the crop, variety (variety) and date; the container is cool, dark and protected from moisture; and you have chosen several healthy parent plants.

english.heading: Field Action
body: Select.
Process.
Protect.
Verify.
Those four actions carry a seed collection from this field into the next season.
Begin with one crop and do it well.
Which crop will you begin with?
Say it aloud. Then choose one action you will take next.
The next season is already inside the seed you choose today.

heading.text: Ketso ya Tshimong

body.text: Kgetha.
body.backTranslation: Choose.

body.text: Lokisa (process).
body.backTranslation: Prepare (process).

body.text: Sireletsa.
body.backTranslation: Protect.

body.text: Netefatsa.
body.backTranslation: Confirm.

body.text: Diketso tseo tse nne di isa pokello ya peo ho tswa tshimong ena ho fihlela sehla se latelang.
body.backTranslation: Those four actions carry the seed collection from this field until the next season.

body.text: Qala ka sejalo se le seng mme o se etse hantle.
body.backTranslation: Start with one crop and do it well.

body.text: O tla qala ka sejalo sefe?
body.backTranslation: Which crop will you start with?

body.text: E bolele ka lentswe le phahameng. Ebe o kgetha ketso e le nngwe eo o tla e etsa e latelang.
body.backTranslation: Say it out loud. Then choose one action that you will do next.

body.text: Sehla se latelang se se se ka hare ho peo eo o e kgethang kajeno.
body.backTranslation: The coming season is already inside the seed you choose today.
